title: A hand-rolled session parser desyncs on an attacker-chosen key name, and a later unserialize assembles the object from two request fields
index_line: T-0029 · EXEC · key name corrupts the session framing; the uploaded filename supplies the next bytes; a second unserialize fires the gadget · php · corroborated
invariant_violated: The session store is assumed to be integrity-protected because the attacker never gets to send a serialized object: the framework writes it, the server reads it. But the framework's own hand-rolled reader trusts the *shape* of what it parses, so a key name that desynchronises its pointer lets an attacker append entries — and a second location that unserializes a stored string turns those entries into an object stream.

mechanism.does: an authenticated low-privilege user sends an upload request whose `from` parameter becomes the name of a key written into the session
the session layer re-serializes the session with its own parser, which walks the string with a pointer rather than using the language's deserializer
a crafted key (a leading `!`, then closing quotes and delimiter bytes) makes the reader record 'this key has no value' and move on with its pointer misaligned
the misalignment lets the following bytes — supplied by an uploaded file's name — be written into the session as a new entry
the session is stored and later reloaded; a different code path unserializes one of those entries as a serialized blob
the object's magic method runs on destruction or wakeup, and the assembler's own API hands it the attacker string as a command
the configured command executes as the web user, from a request that needed only mailbox credentials

source.http.request.value: the pair of ordinary request fields — a handler-naming parameter and an uploaded file's name — that together form the serialized payload; neither alone carries it

sink.deser.native.value: the second-order unserialize of a value the session now holds (preferences, identity, cached config) — the real sink, not the session load

encoding.object-stream.value: the object stream assembled in two halves: `O:NN:"Class"` in one field, the property bytes in the other

guard.escaping.value: the session parser's framing rules — the guard is the delimiter/pointer discipline, and it is defeated by a key that changes the reader's state

gadget.magic-method.value: a class whose destructor/wakeup treats one of its own properties as an executable command (GPG engine, mail transport, cache backend)

preconditions.expr: sessions are re-serialized by a hand-rolled parser rather than the platform's serializer, and a request parameter becomes a session key
an action writes a request-supplied name into the session and a second place unserializes a session-held string
the attacker holds any mailbox account (post-auth, low privilege) — this is not pre-auth
a usable gadget class is autoloadable (the framework ships ones whose destructor runs a configured command)

success: the session store shows an entry the request never legitimately set, adjacent to the key the parameter named
the command's side effect appears on the next request that reloads the session — the payload lands at load time, not at upload time
the object stream in the store contains a class name the application never instantiates for that key
failure_like: the session layer uses the platform serializer and/or validates the key against an allow-list before use
the second-order unserialize passes `allowed_classes => false`, so the stream becomes arrays only
false_positive: a session entry that looks odd because of a legitimate framework upgrade or a stale entry — compare against a control request that changes nothing
a deserialization error page proving the payload reached the parser but not that a gadget executed
claiming pre-auth: this needs a mailbox account; the finding starts at PR:L

hazards: the interesting part is the *split* payload: check every place where two request fields are concatenated into one stored value
hand-rolled parsers of serialized formats are the recurring defect — a pointer-walking reader over attacker-influenced keys is a framing bug waiting to happen
gadget availability decides impact: enumerate destructors/wakeups in the framework and its bundled libraries before declaring RCE
related to but distinct from T-0019 (flat store, CRLF record injection): here the framing of a serialization format is desynced, not the record delimiter
non_transfers: frameworks that sign or HMAC the session blob
session keys restricted to an allow-list before any write
serializers that reject a key on the first malformed token and abort the whole load

provenance.author: FearsOff research (Kirill Firsov, CVE-2025-49113 finder)
provenance.corroborates: full chain: the hand-rolled session serializer, the `!` key desync, the uploaded filename as the second half, the second-order unserialize and the working gadget payload

provenance.author: Roundcube (vendor advisory)
provenance.corroborates: affected versions, the `_from` parameter in program/actions/settings/upload.php, and the fix releases
